settingText: Present-day Nuxis archive room, quiet and rain-muted, with ordinary shelves and a sealed window.
summary: Theo and Rae compare fragments from the Desert Marker and realize they remember incompatible emotional versions of the same event. Adrian refuses to decide which memory is true. A shared remembered phrase pulls both of them into the past.

dialogueInline.text: He thought waiting would kill everyone.
Someone was still getting people out.
Both of you stop trying to make the other one wrong.
Then tell us which one happened.

directionInline.text: Keep the present-day frame short and intimate. Theo remembers Starbreaker's fear of waiting; Rae remembers people being moved. Adrian's refusal to privilege either perspective triggers the transition. Once the memory begins, leave the present for most of the issue.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Wide, quiet establishing panel. Nuxis archive room after hours: ordinary physical shelves, a sealed window streaked by rain, low practical lamps, no futuristic spectacle. Theo and Rae sit on opposite sides of a scarred table with copied notes between them; Adrian remains slightly apart.
Panel 2 — Theo leans over the notes but looks past them as he says, 'He thought waiting would kill everyone.' Rae answers from a different emotional memory: 'Someone was still getting people out.'

Panel 3 — Close alternating reactions for 'I didn't see that.' / 'I did.' Their disagreement is unsettling because both are certain. Adrian interrupts: 'Both of you stop trying to make the other one wrong.'
Panel 4 — Theo turns on Adrian: 'Then tell us which one happened.' Adrian answers, 'They both did.' Rae registers that he means it literally, not philosophically.

Panel 5 — Final transition panel. Match the rain-muted room into windblown ancient dust: the table edge becomes a battered war-room surface and the practical lamp becomes hard ancient daylight. The present disappears completely; the early memory contains no visible Theo or Rae.

settingText: Ancient Desert Marker war room before the catastrophe: crowded, worn, inhabited, with open doors to dust and frightened civilians outside.
summary: In the forgotten past, Starbreaker presses Mero for authority to end the Desert Marker threat decisively before it spreads. Mero stalls because Redlin has asked for one final chance to contain the crisis.

dialogueInline.text: If we leave it breathing, it spreads.
And you always ask me to end something.
Because some things only stop when somebody does.
That's what frightens me about you.

directionInline.text: Starbreaker is exhausted and subdued. Mero's authority comes from listening longer than anyone wants him to. The scene is about whether waiting saves lives or merely gives catastrophe room to widen.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Wide ancient establishing panel. The Desert Marker war room is a repurposed civic/work space, not a sleek command bridge: battered tables, hand-marked evacuation routes, dust blowing through open doors, civilians visible beyond. Mero is human-scale; Starbreaker is luminous but visibly exhausted.

Panel 2 — Starbreaker, fractured white-gold-black armor dulled by dust, points toward the worsening horizon outside: 'If we leave it breathing, it spreads.' Mero answers from reports in his hands: 'Redlin asked for time.'
Panel 3 — 'Redlin always asks for time.' / 'And you always ask me to end something.' Hold both men in the same frame; Mero is visually smaller but not less authoritative.
Panel 4 — Starbreaker: 'Because some things only stop when somebody does.' His anger reads as fear converted into decisiveness.
Panel 5 — Final close on Mero: 'That's what frightens me about you.' Behind him, frightened people keep moving through the open doorway. End on the cost that makes both arguments plausible.

settingText: Same ancient war room, moments later, dust blowing in as Redlin returns from the civilian line.
summary: Redlin enters as a full person. He and Starbreaker reveal an old rivalry built on mutual familiarity: Starbreaker believes Redlin keeps catastrophes alive by refusing decisive endings; Redlin believes Starbreaker creates new catastrophes every time he calls one finished.

dialogueInline.text: Still talking about me like I'm late to my own funeral?
People are always leaving when you arrive.
No. We keep saying enough and then meeting again over another burning world.
Maybe because you keep burning them.

directionInline.text: Redlin comes in dirty from helping ordinary people. His first exchange with Starbreaker should imply years of familiarity, respect and accumulated disappointment. Containment reads through Redlin's choices as a moral instinct.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Redlin enters from the civilian line, dark containment armor marked by deep red structural channels, carrying grime and a torn strap from someone else's pack. He looks like he has been helping people, not arriving ceremonially.
Panel 2 — 'Still talking about me like I'm late to my own funeral?' / 'You are late.' Mero watches the familiar rhythm rather than intervening immediately.
Panel 3 — 'People were leaving.' / 'People are always leaving when you arrive.' Redlin answers, 'Because they're still alive.' Keep the exchange dry enough to imply years of history.
Panel 4 — Mero says, 'Enough.' Starbreaker refuses: 'No. We keep saying enough and then meeting again over another burning world.' The old affection has turned into accusation.
Panel 5 — Final two-shot. Redlin: 'Maybe because you keep burning them.' Neither looks away. End on mutual hurt, not hero-versus-villain posturing.

settingText: Ancient civilian shelter beneath the Desert Marker settlement: tired families, packed belongings, people waiting for permission to leave.
summary: Redlin takes Mero through a civilian shelter rather than arguing from a command room. His containment position becomes human: he knows the names of people who will die if Starbreaker acts now.

dialogueInline.text: You brought me here to change my mind.
I brought you here so they weren't numbers when you decide.
And if you can't hold it?
Then I'll know who I failed.

directionInline.text: Use small human details: a child asleep against a stranger, an old person refusing to leave a box, somebody sharing water. Mero already understands the cost; Redlin insists that understanding remain attached to people.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Wide shelter panel at human eye level. Packed families sit beneath old structural ribs with bags, blankets and salvaged belongings. A child sleeps against a stranger; an elderly person grips a battered box; water is passed hand to hand. Redlin and Mero move through them without an entourage.
Panel 2 — Mero: 'You brought me here to change my mind.' Redlin keeps walking: 'I brought you here so they weren't numbers when you decide.'
Panel 3 — 'I don't need that lesson.' / 'Then learn their names anyway.' Redlin stops beside people he plainly recognizes. Show familiarity through acting without inventing lettered dialogue.
Panel 4 — Mero asks, 'And if you can't hold it?' Redlin's attention stays on the civilians rather than the general.
Panel 5 — Final close on Redlin: 'Then I'll know who I failed.' Behind him, the shelter is full of specific faces. End on the burden he is choosing to remember.

settingText: Ancient ridge above the Desert Marker basin, looking toward distant places already ruined by the widening war.
summary: Starbreaker shows Mero what waiting has already cost elsewhere. His decisiveness is rooted in accumulated failure, not appetite for destruction.

dialogueInline.text: No. You looked at maps. Look at what waiting leaves behind.
And you think ending this fixes those places?
I think there can still be places left to fix.

directionInline.text: Show abandoned streets, evacuation fires and ordinary belongings. Starbreaker has carried too many endings he believes could have been prevented. He is frightening because his argument is emotionally understandable.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Large landscape from the ridge. Below: the Desert Marker basin and evacuation routes. Farther away: abandoned streets, evacuation fires, damaged settlements and ordinary belongings left in the road. Cosmic-war scale is expressed through human abandonment.
Panel 2 — Starbreaker, small against the landscape despite his radiance: 'Look past this ridge.' Mero: 'I have.'
Panel 3 — 'No. You looked at maps. Look at what waiting leaves behind.' The evidence is the landscape itself, not tactical graphics. Mero asks, 'And you think ending this fixes those places?'
Panel 4 — Starbreaker looks toward a distant evacuation column: 'I think there can still be places left to fix.' His fatigue makes the line tragic rather than triumphant.
Panel 5 — Final silent image: a child's abandoned object or family keepsake lies half-buried in ridge dust between them, linking Starbreaker's argument to the civilians Redlin just showed Mero.

settingText: Ancient Desert Marker war room, later, with the outside crisis pressing visibly closer.
summary: Mero tries to broker a pause. Starbreaker and Redlin reveal that each believes the other's signature virtue has become a vice.

dialogueInline.text: One hour. Both of you stand down.
And every time you cut it short.
Every time you mistake delay for mercy.
Every time you mistake an ending for a solution.
Do either of you remember how to speak to each other without a battlefield between you?

directionInline.text: Let this feel like an old relationship worn raw by repeated crises. Mero's question should register as grief for who these people were before the war made every disagreement existential.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Return to the battered war room, visibly worse: thicker dust through the doors, more empty civilian places, a damaged wall, messengers moving quickly. Mero stands between Starbreaker and Redlin instead of behind a command table.
Panel 2 — 'One hour. Both of you stand down.' / 'We've had this hour before.' The request lands as a repetition all three men recognize.

Panel 3 — 'And every time you cut it short.' / 'Every time you mistake delay for mercy.' / 'Every time you mistake an ending for a solution.' Use close opposing profiles; they know exactly where to hurt each other.
Panel 4 — Mero: 'Do either of you remember how to speak to each other without a battlefield between you?' This is grief for who they were, not a rhetorical command.
Panel 5 — Final close on Redlin looking at Starbreaker: 'I do. That's the problem.' Starbreaker's reaction reveals that he remembers too.

settingText: Ancient outer evacuation line at the Desert Marker settlement, dust and panic, kept close to civilians.
summary: Redlin personally holds the outer line long enough for civilians to move. The sequence defines containment as protection and endurance rather than technology.

dialogueInline.text: Don't look back at me. Look at the person in front of you.

directionInline.text: Redlin takes weight from an injured stranger, steadies someone who has frozen, and stays where danger is arriving. The point is simple: keep the disaster from reaching the next person.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Wide horizontal panel at the outer evacuation line. Civilians move through dust between damaged structures while danger advances from the opposite direction. Redlin stands at the rear of the flow, not at the front like a conquering hero.
Panel 2 — Redlin takes an injured stranger's weight: 'Keep moving.' His containment armor bears strain and damage; the effect reads through physical endurance, not a diagram.
Panel 3 — A frightened civilian turns toward danger. Redlin: 'Don't look back at me. Look at the person in front of you.' The instruction creates a chain of people helping one another.
Panel 4 — Redlin physically places a small child into another adult's arms: 'Take the child. Both hands.' Then, 'Good. Now go.' The civilian leaves; Redlin stays.
Panel 5 — Large final panel. The evacuation line recedes behind Redlin as he turns alone toward the arriving catastrophe. End on endurance, not a power pose.

settingText: Ancient ridge in a brief lull, with the settlement below and the broken sky beyond.
summary: Starbreaker and Redlin meet alone before the final break. Their hostility falls away long enough to reveal old respect. Each asks the other to stop. Neither can.

dialogueInline.text: You know what happens if I wait.
I know what happens when you don't.
I used to trust you to know when enough was enough.
I used to trust you to know the difference between courage and impatience.
Then we both remember better days.

directionInline.text: Play the exchange privately, almost quietly. Seed deeper history without defining the unresolved betrayal. Both still care what the other thinks, which makes the break worse.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Quiet wide panel on the ridge. The settlement and broken sky fill the distance, but Starbreaker and Redlin stand only a few feet apart. Remove soldiers and spectacle; this is a private conversation inside a public catastrophe.
Panel 2 — 'You could move.' / 'So could you.' Their posture is tired, familiar, almost conversational.
Panel 3 — 'You know what happens if I wait.' / 'I know what happens when you don't.' Keep both faces readable; neither is posturing.

Panel 4 — Starbreaker: 'I used to trust you to know when enough was enough.' Redlin: 'I used to trust you to know the difference between courage and impatience.' Both lines expose grief rather than contempt.
Panel 5 — Final two-shot against the broken sky. 'Then we both remember better days.' Neither moves aside. End on two people who still care and cannot yield.

settingText: Ancient Desert Marker battlefield at the instant the crisis becomes irreversible.
summary: The crisis crosses the point where every available choice carries catastrophe. Starbreaker acts, Redlin keeps trying to protect what remains, and the sky begins to break.

directionInline.text: The sky behaves impossibly; distant structures fold into light; people understand danger before they understand cause. Frame the moment as two incompatible forms of courage colliding.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Wide battlefield panel. Distant structures bend or collapse into impossible light, dust lifts against gravity, civilians react before they understand why. Keep the phenomenon experiential, never diagrammed.
Panel 2 — Mero sees Starbreaker make the decision and says only, 'Starbreaker.' The human general is too far away to physically stop him.
Panel 3 — Tight on Starbreaker, exhausted and afraid: 'I know.' His first-light weapon forms as fractured, controlled stellar radiance rather than a generic beam.
Panel 4 — Redlin reaches him: 'Don't.' Starbreaker: 'Then hold it.' Redlin braces between the act and the remaining evacuation line: 'I'm trying.' Show people behind him, not abstract field graphics.

Panel 5 — Large final panel. Starbreaker's decisive light and Redlin's holding action meet; the sky fractures into unnatural geometry above them. End at the instant before the full consequence, with Mero and civilians small enough to preserve scale and stakes.

settingText: Ancient Desert Marker aftermath under falling glass dust and violet light.
summary: Starbreaker believes he prevented something worse; Redlin is looking at the people who still died. Mero understands that both statements can be true.

dialogueInline.text: No. You're looking at what didn't happen.
And you're looking only at what did.
That's how this war keeps us.

directionInline.text: Let silence and aftermath do most of the work. Let the aftermath expose the war's trap: each side can point to real lives saved by its logic and real lives destroyed by the other's failure.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Full-width aftermath. Glass-like dust falls slowly through violet light over a shattered settlement. Survivors search debris, injured people are carried, some evacuation routes remain intact, others simply end. No triumphant composition.
Panel 2 — Starbreaker stands emptied out, radiance reduced: 'It stopped.' Redlin, helping a survivor: 'Look around you.' Starbreaker: 'I am.'
Panel 3 — Redlin: 'No. You're looking at what didn't happen.' Frame him with the dead and wounded he could not save.
Panel 4 — Mero: 'And you're looking only at what did.' Show surviving civilians moving through the same frame so his point is visual, not abstract.
Panel 5 — Final quiet three-shot beneath falling glass dust. Mero: 'That's how this war keeps us.' Starbreaker and Redlin cannot answer. End with neither vindicated.

settingText: Present-day Nuxis archive room, the memory gone and ordinary rain still against the window.
summary: Theo and Rae return carrying different human details from the same day. Neither understands why the same scene belongs to both of them.

dialogueInline.text: I remember Redlin carrying a little girl.

directionInline.text: Compare intimate details, not lore. The reader should not yet realize that the memories have had their autobiographical subject removed.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Hard return to the same Nuxis archive composition from Page 1. Rain still moves down the sealed window; almost no present time has passed. Theo and Rae are both physically shaken, but differently.
Panel 2 — Theo, staring at his hands: 'He was afraid.' Rae: 'Redlin?' Theo: 'Starbreaker.' The revelation is emotional: the terrifying champion was afraid.
Panel 3 — Rae: 'I remember Redlin carrying a little girl.' Theo: 'I don't.' Her memory is tactile and specific, not a lore summary.
Panel 4 — Rae: 'I don't remember the ridge.' Hold a two-shot as they understand that their memories overlap without matching.

Panel 5 — Final silent insert on their separate notes: two partial accounts of the same day, each containing intimate details the other lacks. Keep the autobiographical viewpoint absent; the missing point of view remains the mystery.

settingText: Present-day maintenance hatch opening onto ordinary rain and city light.
summary: Theo and Rae ask how two people can remember private details from the same forgotten day. Adrian refuses the identity truth but confirms that neither memory is false.

dialogueInline.text: How can we remember the same day from different places?
Because a day doesn't belong to one person.

directionInline.text: Adrian is not being playfully cryptic. He is actively postponing a truth he believes they are not ready to survive. End on Rae recognizing that refusal is not denial.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Theo, Rae and Adrian step through a maintenance hatch into ordinary rain and city light. Cosmic memory collapses back to wet pavement, service rails and mundane night traffic. Keep all three grounded.
Panel 2 — Theo: 'How can we remember the same day from different places?' Adrian avoids looking at either of them: 'Because a day doesn't belong to one person.'
Panel 3 — Rae: 'That's not what he asked.' Adrian: 'I know.' His restraint reads as fear of consequence, not smug mystery.
Panel 4 — Theo stops walking: 'Were either of us there?' Adrian turns back, visibly burdened: 'Not tonight.' Leave space around the refusal so it registers as a choice.
Panel 5 — Final close on Rae watching him: 'That's not a no.' Adrian does not answer. End on Rae understanding that his refusal confirms the direction of the truth without revealing it.
